articles.markdown:
---
title: "A Pod is not its container"
dek: "A container can restart without a Pod being replaced. A Pod can be replaced without an application being redeployed. Those two identities explain the resource tree, the restart counter and the controller's job."
handbook: kubernetes
phase: 1
lab: labs/pod-lifecycle
sources:
  - id: pod-lifecycle
    author: "Kubernetes Authors"
    year: "current"
    title: "Pod Lifecycle"
    where: "Kubernetes documentation"
    url: "https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/"
    note: "The distinction between Pod identity, container restarts, phases and display status."
  - id: resources
    author: "Kubernetes Authors"
    year: "current"
    title: "Resource Management for Pods and Containers"
    where: "Kubernetes documentation"
    url: "https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/"
    note: "Requests determine placement; limits constrain resource consumption."
  - id: deployments
    author: "Kubernetes Authors"
    year: "current"
    title: "Deployments"
    where: "Kubernetes documentation"
    url: "https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/"
    note: "Replica counts, Pod templates and the explicitly selected Recreate strategy."
---

A restart counter goes up while the Pod's UID stays put. Delete that Pod, and its replacement has a different UID. The container and the Pod have different lifetimes. Kubernetes schedules each Pod once; a replacement is another object, even if it does the same job. [Pod lifetime](#src-pod-lifecycle)

## The owner matters

A standalone Pod has no controller responsible for replacing it. A Deployment uses ReplicaSets to maintain a desired replica count. Changing `replicas` changes that count; changing the Pod template starts a rollout. The lab explicitly selects `Recreate`, which removes old Pods before starting the new revision. It does not simulate the default RollingUpdate strategy. [Deployments](#src-deployments)

## Placement is not consumption

Requests reserve schedulable capacity. Limits constrain consumption. A low CPU limit can throttle a container; exceeding a memory limit can lead to an OOM kill. Neither setting itself scales replicas. [Resource management](#src-resources)

## Read the two status fields

`Pending` and `Running` are Pod phases. `ImagePullBackOff`, `CrashLoopBackOff` and `Terminating` are useful display statuses, not additional phases. Read the waiting or termination reason alongside the phase. [Pod status](#src-pod-lifecycle)

> [!deeper] Why can a scheduled Pod still be Pending?
>
> Binding chooses a node; it does not prove the container has started. An image-pull failure can leave a bound Pod waiting. In the lab, its node badge and reserved capacity remain while the display reports ImagePullBackOff. The reason explains more than the phase alone. [Container states](#src-pod-lifecycle)

questions.prompt: A container is OOM-killed and restarted inside a Pod. What happens to the Pod UID?
questions.explanation: A container restart and a Pod replacement are different events. Restarting the container preserves the Pod identity and node assignment. A replacement Pod is a new API object with a new UID.

review.notes: Original practice question. An educator should review factual accuracy, distractors and objective alignment.

questions.remediation: Load “Memory limit exceeded” in the lab, advance time and compare the Pod UID with its container restart counter.

options.explanation: Correct. The kubelet can restart the container within the existing Pod.

options.text: Every container restart creates a new Pod UID.
options.explanation: This confuses a container restart with replacement of the Pod object.

options.text: The existing Pod moves to another node.
options.explanation: An existing Pod is not rescheduled onto another node. A replacement is a different Pod.

questions.prompt: Select every correct statement about requests and limits in this lab.
questions.explanation: The scheduler places Pods using requests. Limits constrain runtime use: CPU may be throttled and a memory limit can lead to an OOM kill. Neither setting changes the desired replica count. The lab models these qualitatively.

review.notes: Original practice question. An educator should review factual accuracy, distractors and objective alignment.

questions.remediation: Keep replicas unchanged, raise a CPU request, then change a memory limit and observe the different effects.

options.text: CPU and memory requests are used for placement.
options.explanation: Correct. The scheduler checks whether a node can satisfy the requested resources.

options.text: Exceeding a memory limit can cause the container to be OOM-killed.
options.explanation: Correct. The lab demonstrates an OOM kill followed by restart under its restart policy.

options.text: Raising a CPU limit creates extra replicas.
options.explanation: A CPU limit does not change spec.replicas. This lab has no HPA.

options.text: A CPU request is a measurement of current CPU usage.
options.explanation: A request is a scheduling/resource reservation input, not a live usage measurement.

questions.prompt: Order a successful startup in this lab, from creation to ready. Its model uses two fixed startup steps and no probes.
questions.explanation: The ReplicaSet creates a Pod; the scheduler binds it to one node; the kubelet starts its container; the lab then marks it Ready. Real startup timing and readiness depend on the workload and cluster.

review.notes: Original practice question. An educator should review factual accuracy, distractors and objective alignment.

questions.remediation: Load “Healthy deployment”, rewind the history and inspect the Created, Scheduled and Started events.

items.text: Pod becomes Ready in the lab
Scheduler binds the Pod to a node

questions.prompt: Match each responsibility to the component that performs it. Targets may be used more than once.
questions.explanation: Desired count, node assignment and container management are separate responsibilities. The resource tree shows ownership; the node badge shows a scheduling assignment.

review.notes: Original practice question. An educator should review factual accuracy, distractors and objective alignment.

questions.remediation: Delete a selected Pod and inspect which events concern creation, scheduling and starting.

items.text: Creates a replacement to maintain the replica count
items.explanation: The ReplicaSet controller reconciles actual Pod count with desired replicas.

items.text: Selects a node for a new unscheduled Pod
items.explanation: The scheduler binds an unscheduled Pod to a suitable node.

items.text: Ensures the container starts on the assigned node
items.explanation: The kubelet manages containers on its node.

questions.prompt: Each of the two lab nodes has 2000m allocatable CPU and no reservations. What happens to a Pod using this container resource fragment?
questions.explanation: A Pod must fit on a single node. A 3000m request cannot fit either 2000m node, even though their combined free CPU is 4000m. Placement uses the request, not the limit.

review.notes: Original practice question. An educator should review factual accuracy, distractors and objective alignment.

questions.remediation: Apply a 3000m CPU request with a 4000m limit. Inspect Pending and the node reservation gauges.

options.text: It remains Pending because neither node can fit the CPU request.
options.explanation: Correct. The request is checked against each candidate node separately.

options.text: It runs by combining free CPU across both nodes.
options.explanation: A single Pod cannot split its CPU request across nodes.

options.text: It reserves 4000m because placement uses limits.
options.explanation: Placement uses requests. The CPU limit constrains runtime use rather than declaring a scheduling reservation.

questions.code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 3000m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 4000m
    memory: 512Mi

questions.prompt: You delete a Pod owned by the lab Deployment while its desired replicas remain two. What should you observe after reconciliation?
questions.explanation: The ReplicaSet observes a missing replica and creates another Pod. The replacement has a new UID. With a standalone Pod, no ReplicaSet maintains that count.

review.notes: Original practice question. An educator should review factual accuracy, distractors and objective alignment.

questions.remediation: Compare “Healthy deployment” with “A Pod without a controller” and delete a selected Pod in each.

options.text: A replacement Pod appears with a new UID.
options.explanation: Correct. Reconciliation restores the desired count with a new object.

options.text: The deleted Pod returns with the same UID.
options.explanation: An API object that was deleted is not the same object as its replacement.

options.text: Deleting the child also deletes its ReplicaSet.
options.explanation: Deleting one owned Pod does not delete its controller.

questions.prompt: The lab uses restartPolicy Always. Its synthetic container working set is 192 Mi. What does this resource fragment demonstrate?
questions.explanation: The synthetic working set exceeds the 128Mi limit. The lab kills and restarts the container with backoff; the Pod UID and scheduling reservation remain. The 64Mi request governs placement, not the runtime maximum.

review.notes: Original practice question. An educator should review factual accuracy, distractors and objective alignment.

questions.remediation: Choose “Memory limit exceeded”, watch restarts, then lower the synthetic working set to 96 Mi.

options.text: The container is OOM-killed and may restart inside the same Pod.
options.explanation: Correct. Under this lab policy the container restarts, preserving the Pod identity.

options.text: The container stops using memory at exactly its 64Mi request.
options.explanation: The request is not a hard runtime memory ceiling.

options.text: The same Pod moves to another node to escape the limit.
options.explanation: Changing nodes is not how an existing Pod responds to a container memory limit.

questions.code:

    memory: 64Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 1000m
    memory: 128Mi
